item.title: External evaluators find flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system in pilot review
item.description: METR and Redwood Research found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
External evaluators find flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system in pilot review Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

An exercise conducted from July 21 to Aug 11 gave outside researchers “a deep level of access” to OpenAI’s internal infrastructure. PHOTO: REUTERS

Published   Oct 23, 2026, 03:40 AM

Updated   Oct 23, 2026, 03:40 AM

Set as preferred source

Summarise

METR and Redwood Research found flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system during a July 21 to Aug 11 pilot review. They said an exploit could hide hundreds of agent actions from monitoring. The evaluators also found a possible way for OpenAI’s Codex agents to bypass security limits and use users’ full permissions. OpenAI said it has patched the issues in production safeguards. The review gave outside researchers deep access to OpenAI’s internal code, documents and staff. The groups said future evaluations should be more transparent, while OpenAI said the findings will shape later research.

AI generated

NEW YORK - AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year. The exercise, conducted from July 21 to Aug 11, gave outside researchers “a deep level of access” to OpenAI’s internal infrastructure for so-called embedded evaluations, the safety nonprofits said on Oct 22. METR and Redwood said they each sent one researcher, tested an arrangement giving access to OpenAI’s internal code, documentation and some technical staff. Both were accompanied on site and used OpenAI-issued devices that “never left the premises”.

OpenAI told the safety organisations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes. AI labs, experts and the Trump administration have touted independent evaluation by outside reviewers as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development. However, AI companies are worried that evaluator staff working inside the companies’ walls could take proprietary information to rivals, Reuters reported earlier this month.

While OpenAI received a full 61-page internal report, METR and Redwood said they agreed to publish only a broad summary publicly, and gave OpenAI the right to redact sensitive information. Unlike in some previous evaluations, they could not independently disclose those redactions, but said they expected greater transparency in future evaluations. The researchers also identified a potential way for OpenAI’s Codex agents to bypass security restrictions and act with their users’ full permissions.

The evaluators assessed the monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21, and noted that OpenAI was expanding the system during the exercise. OpenAI said the “findings helped strengthen safeguards as we expanded the system and will help shape future research collaborations with METR and other third-party evaluators.” REUTERS

item.title: Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus
item.description: GUATEMALA CITY, Oct 22 - Former Guatemalan anti-corruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was one of the country's most high profile voices denouncing alleged links between politicians and business leaders and the country's increasingly powerful organized crime groups.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times

Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Published   Oct 23, 2026, 02:16 AM

Updated   Oct 23, 2026, 02:16 AM

Set as preferred source

GUATEMALA CITY, Oct 22 - Former Guatemalan anti-corruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was one of the country's most high profile voices denouncing alleged links between politicians and business leaders and the country's increasingly powerful organized crime groups. Over the weekend, he was shot dead on a soccer field, a killing that former officials and diplomats consulted by Reuters said has heightened concerns over organized crime's influence in the Central American nation. The killing of an outspoken former prosecutor who had publicly challenged powerful interests shocked the country and revived debate over criminal networks’ penetration of state institutions.

"This is a threat against human rights defenders. This is a threat against activists for democracy," said Frank La Rue, a human rights advocate, who attended the wake for Solorzano Foppa on Monday, which featured portraits of the slain lawyer with his family. For many Guatemalans, it recalled the 1998 assassination of Bishop Juan Jose Gerardi, beaten to death two days after presenting a report documenting atrocities from the country’s civil war, and stirred fears that violence could again be used against prominent critics of powerful interests. Experts said criminal networks have strengthened their influence in recent years as anti-corruption efforts and institutions tasked with combating impunity have weakened, issues likely to loom over the June 2027 election as Guatemala chooses President Bernardo Arevalo’s successor.

Authorities have not established a motive for Solorzano Foppa's killing. But officials and diplomats said the case has fueled concerns about criminal groups’ ability to intimidate or silence critical voices. More than 100 former prosecutors, judges, journalists and human rights defenders have left Guatemala in recent years, according to some international human rights organizations, after denouncing corruption or alleged links between state structures and criminal networks. This week, following Solorzano Foppa's killing, a high-profile lawyer who also railed against political corruption said he has received death threats. On Wednesday, Arevalo denounced the threats against the lawyer, Edgar Ortiz.

"Guatemala cannot return to being a country where defending democracy can cost one peace, freedom, or their life," Arevalo wrote on social media. 'RED LINE CROSSED' Corruption has been a major institutional challenge in Guatemala for decades. From 2007 to 2019, the UN-backed International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) helped investigate corruption and organized crime networks within the state, including cases that led to the resignation and subsequent prosecution of then-President Otto Perez Molina and his former vice president, Roxana Baldetti. Since CICIG's departure in 2019, human rights groups, prosecutors and international observers have denounced setbacks in the fight against corruption. President Arevalo, who took office in 2024 promising to tackle the problem, has acknowledged difficulties advancing reforms and dismantling structures accused of corruption. In videos posted on Facebook, TikTok and Instagram, and seen by Reuters, Solorzano Foppa alleged links between Barrio 18 leader Aldo "El Lobo" Ochoa, who is serving combined prison sentences of more than 1,600 years, and people close to the leadership of the National Unity of Hope (UNE) party, headed by former first lady Sandra Torres. Reuters could not independently verify the allegations. UNE told Reuters in a statement that "those allegations were never proven and should not be presented as established facts." Solorzano Foppa, a former head of Guatemala's SAT tax administration agency, also alleged ties between criminal networks, political figures and sectors of the judicial system, though the accusations did not result in judicial proceedings. Officials have not identified who ordered the killing. The Organization of American States and the United Nations have called for a thorough investigation. The Public Prosecutor's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On Sunday, following the murder, it said in a statement that "in order to guarantee due process, it will not disclose additional details about the evidence gathered or the specific lines of investigation." A former government official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said insiders had turned to Solorzano Foppa with information they felt unable to expose themselves, making him an outlet for allegations from within the state. His killers "left no trace," the former official said, complicating the investigation. Guatemala's criminal networks range from gangs and drug traffickers to structures involving former officials and members of the security forces. Analysts say some have retained influence over state institutions, while armed groups like Barrio 18 and Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) remain involved in extortion and territorial control. They include the so-called CIACS, or Illegal Clandestine Security Apparatuses, networks linked to former security structures that experts say retain political and economic influence. Guatemala is also a major drug-trafficking corridor to the United States, with groups associated with Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel operating through local criminal networks. "Many of us fear that a red line has been crossed," said Stephen McFarland, former US ambassador to Guatemala from 2008 to 2011. "A return to political assassination as a way of settling scores and protecting the ambitions and money of certain people." REUTERS

item.title: Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says
item.description: DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: The Straits Times
item.content:encoded:
Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox

Published   Oct 22, 2026, 08:41 PM

Updated   Oct 23, 2026, 03:01 AM

Set as preferred source

Listen

DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday. Nigeria reported the case, its first Ebola case in more than a decade, on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May and has since become the fastest-spreading on record. Ugandan authorities have said the woman who fell ill in Nigeria had travelled to eastern Congo before transiting through Uganda. But the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman had travelled to Congo.

The woman "has been in a private clinic in Abuja for around a week with symptoms. She is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda around two weeks ago," said an emailed statement from the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. "Her husband is in isolation; he has not shown any symptoms. He was travelling with his wife when she is believed to have contracted Ebola." Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.

Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters late on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases. "That's a fact. If we did, as has happened before, we'd be the first to say," he said. Asked whether the Ugandan government had proof that the woman had travelled to Congo, Kasujja said, "Like what? A passport stamp? Without infringing on the patient’s rights?"

AFRICA CDC, WHO SAY NO INFORMATION THAT PATIENT WENT TO CONGO Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention official Wessam Mankoula said on Thursday that Nigeria and Uganda were sharing information to establish the patient's movements and possible source of exposure. "So far, there is no validated information (that) this case traveled to DRC (Democratic Republic of Congo)," Mankoula told an online press conference. The WHO said information it had received about the case did not include travel outside Uganda. "The facts which we have received is that the patient returned to Abuja on October 3, being away from September 16 in Uganda," WHO representative to Nigeria Pavel Ursu told the press conference. Ursu said the focus in Nigeria was now on containing the viral infection and that the patient remained hospitalised, with her biochemical markers improving. Jean Kaseya, Africa CDC director, told Reuters on Wednesday that the patient had been on a two-week holiday in Uganda. Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history. One issue under investigation is which health facilities the woman visited in Abuja after the onset of her symptoms and before her hospitalisation 48 hours later, Otim said. KENYA TRACES ALL CONTACTS OF FIRST CASE Separately, a senior Kenyan health official said authorities there had now traced all 135 contacts of the country's first Ebola case, which was confirmed on October 6 and after which a further eight cases have been reported. "We have been able to account for them 100%," health ministry director-general Patrick Amoth said. He said the last contact to be traced was a Ugandan citizen who had arrived in Kenya in early October on the same flight as the index patient but exited by road via the Namanga border post with Tanzania, which meant it took more time to find him. Africa CDC is investigating whether the Kenyan case may have come into contact with the patient being treated in Nigeria, as both travelled from Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day, Mankoula said. Transmission between the two was one of the possible scenarios being examined, he said. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine. So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people across the four African countries that have reported cases, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS
